name: AI and Environmental Sustainability
description: This course is for students, early-career professionals, and lifelong learners with an interest in how AI can shape—and be shaped by—environmental sustainability goals. It is particularly valuable for individuals working or aspiring to work in environmental policy, sustainable development, or related fields, who want to understand AI’s potentials and pitfalls in the context of environmental and societal well-being. This course will enhance knowledge about the ethical and political implications of AI in environmental contexts, by connecting the dots of knowledge and information. We welcome a diverse community of learners who value interdisciplinary approaches to complex global challenges. With insights from the social sciences and humanities, this course explore AI-based solutions' broader context and implications.

audience.audienceType: students, early-career professionals, and lifelong learners with an interest in how AI can shape—and be shaped by—environmental sustainability goals

teaches: Making sense of modern AI
AI from a lifecycle perspective
AI from an environmental justice perspective
governing AI's environmental impact

name: Frugal Artificial Intelligence (AI) training course
description: A one-day training course on frugal artificial intelligence, teaching participants to understand and reduce the environmental and social impacts of AI.
abstract: Covers the fundamentals of responsible digital practices, key AI impact areas via the three pillars of Green IT (data centers, hardware, software), and current best-practice solutions for lowering AI's footprint, ending with a concrete organizational action plan.

Understand the environmental and social impacts of current AI

name: MIT 6.5940 TinyML and Efficient Deep Learning Computing
description: This course focuses on efficient machine learning and systems, introducing techniques that enable powerful deep learning applications on resource-constrained devices.
abstract: Topics include model compression, pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, distributed training, data/model parallelism, gradient compression, and on-device fine-tuning, plus application-specific acceleration for large language models and diffusion models. Students get hands-on experience implementing model compression techniques and deploying LLMs (Llama2-7B) on a laptop.

audience.audienceType: Graduate-level students with computer architecture and intro ML background

competencyRequired: MIT 6.191 Computation Structures and 6.390 Intro to Machine Learning (or equivalent prior experience)
license: Not stated on the page (Lecture videos publicly posted on YouTube; slides on course site; not offered Fall 2025 (instructor sabbatical))

abstract: Teaches practitioners the SCI for AI specification, a standard for making the carbon footprint of AI systems (classical and generative) transparent, comparable, and actionable across the AI lifecycle.

abstract: Analyses the full life cycle of an electronic device and covers effective strategies for collecting, sorting and recycling e-waste, circular economy principles for reducing waste and promoting sustainable design, and digital tools (including generative AI) for mapping material flows and assessing environmental impact.

name: Energy Efficient Programming
description: A self-paced openHPI course on writing energy-efficient code in C and assembly, covering computer architecture fundamentals, x86 coding techniques, intrinsics/macros, and hands-on energy measurement with Intel VTune Profiler.
abstract: The course starts from the observation that efficiency in computer science is usually framed as runtime or memory usage, then reframes it around energy consumption. It progresses from computer-architecture basics (clock cycles, parallelism, pipelines, superscalar execution) and x86 programming in week one, to concrete C and assembly coding techniques, SIMD/SSE instruction extensions, and vector intrinsics for reducing instruction count and energy draw in week two, finishing with a practical exercise measuring program energy consumption via Intel's VTune Profiler.
timeRequired: P2W (approx. 5-10 hours per week, 2 weeks — i.e. roughly PT10H to PT20H total, self-paced)

audience.audienceType: Students, researchers, or developers who work or study in computer science or a related field and want to learn energy-efficient coding techniques

teaches: Understand the basic concepts of computer functionality and architecture (clock cycles, parallelism, execution pipelines, superscalar architectures)
Use coding techniques in C and assembly to significantly minimize the number of instructions executed by the CPU
Understand intrinsics and macros and how to apply them to any algorithm to increase its energy efficiency
Measure the energy consumption of programs using the Intel VTune Profiler tool

name: Sustainable Software Engineering (CS4575)
description: A TU Delft MSc course on sustainable software engineering, covering environmental, social, and individual sustainability across the software lifecycle, with a strong Green Software Engineering component on measuring and improving energy efficiency. All lecture slides, schedule, and course materials are published openly on GitHub under an MIT licence.
abstract: Sustainable Software Engineering is an overarching discipline that addresses the long-term consequences of designing, building, and releasing a software project. The course covers a set of competencies needed to leverage sustainable software systems, with a strong component on Green Software Engineering covering techniques to measure and improve energy efficiency at any stage of the software lifecycle, alongside core principles of empirical software engineering and social/individual sustainability.
timeRequired: Not stated in ISO 8601 form; runs one academic quarter (Q3), 5.0 ECTS, three sessions per week
learningResourceType: university course (materials openly published; formal enrolment via TU Delft MSc programmes, but slides/schedule/GitHub repo are freely accessible)

audience.audienceType: Students of the MSc Computer Science and the MSc Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Technology programmes at TU Delft; openly usable by any self-learner via the published GitHub materials

competencyRequired: Intermediate understanding of object-oriented programming languages
Basic understanding of data analysis techniques
teaches: Explain the fundamental sustainability principles and their relevance to software engineering
Assess the energy consumption of software systems using measurement and testing techniques
Create actionable strategies to address sustainability issues within software organisations
Evaluate solutions for sustainable software systems based on their effectiveness and stakeholder impact

name: Sustainable Software Engineering
description: A free, self-paced two-week openHPI course on resource-efficient software engineering, covering climate-friendly decisions across the software development lifecycle with a practical, Python-based second half on writing resource-efficient code.
abstract: The course opens by examining the ecological footprint of digitization — how IT both helps reduce CO2 and contributes to it — and surveys the roles common in the IT industry (developer, IT architect, team lead) to identify where each role can act on resource efficiency. The second week covers the barriers that hinder more ecological action in software development and concrete solutions a developer can apply, using Python for the hands-on material because it is widely known, not because it is a particularly efficient language.
timeRequired: P2W (approx. 3-6 hours per week, 2 weeks — i.e. roughly PT6H to PT12H total, self-paced)

audience.audienceType: Software Developers, Software Architects, Product Owners, and anyone interested in sustainable software engineering

competencyRequired: Basic knowledge of programming in Python
teaches: Understand the ecological footprint of digitization, including how IT both helps reduce and contributes to CO2 emissions
Identify opportunities for resource-efficient action across common IT industry roles (developer, IT architect, team lead)
Recognize the barriers that hinder more ecological action in software development and how to overcome them
Apply concrete, hands-on techniques (in Python) to develop software in a more climate-friendly way

name: Green software use on HPC
description: An introduction to environmental sustainability principles in the context of high performance computing systems
abstract: This lesson introduces environmental sustainability principles in the context of HPC systems. It covers understanding the scale of emissions from different sources, quantifying emissions from HPC use, and practical examples using real data from the ARCHER2 facility. Topics include carbon efficiency, energy efficiency, carbon awareness, hardware efficiency, measurement, and reducing emissions.

audience.audienceType: Anyone involved in using or delivering HPC resources — users, software developers, HPC service operators, and those involved in procuring HPC systems. No knowledge of environmental sustainability principles assumed.

competencyRequired: Familiarity with the key concepts in climate change and green software engineering (covered in the setup section)
teaches: Understand carbon efficiency and how it relates to energy efficiency, including cases where they can conflict
Know how HPC systems can potentially reduce emissions
Understand carbon intensity of electricity generation and implications for carbon-aware HPC use
Appreciate embodied emissions associated with HPC hardware
Be aware of frameworks for measuring and reporting carbon emissions in the context of HPC
Gain practical advice on measuring and improving the carbon efficiency of HPC use

name: Digital Research Sustainability
description: This lesson provides an introduction to digital research sustainability. Digital research practices involve a number of activities that can lead to carbon emissions. This lesson is designed to identify such activities and provide practical ways to reduce the emissions.
abstract:
We will use case studies to explore the carbon impact of digital research activities in four different contexts. Each case study will include some action items that can be implemented to reduce the associated emissions.
After completing this lesson, you should be able to: Explain the big picture for reducing carbon emissions and how that applies to digital research Understand the difference between energy and power, how energy is produced, what are low-carbon energy sources and how they operate Explain what embodied carbon is Use the greenhouse gas (GHG) protocol to estimate carbon emissions Identify which aspects of a research workflow are most carbon‑intensive and why Explore ways to measure and estimate carbon emissions from research software development Identify tools and resources to help estimate emissions associated with daily computational research tasks Explore ways to measure and estimate carbon emissions from High Performance Computing clusters

audience.audienceType: Researchers who write code, Research Software Engineers, Lab scientists who do computational work, Researchers who use HPC, Researchers who use GPUs

teaches: Explain the big picture for reducing carbon emissions and how that applies to digital research
Understand the difference between energy and power, how energy is produced, what are low-carbon energy sources and how they operate

abstract: From the basics of climate science to the advanced applications of green computing and artificial intelligence, this course explores the wide range of challenges and opportunities that IT offers in the fight against climate change. Nine invited experts share diverse perspectives through English-language scientific presentations and German interviews, all fully subtitled. Participants explore practical examples of companies integrating sustainability and collaborate on a shared mission.
